quiz.title: Chapter 8 Quiz: Researching Across Sources
quiz.intro: Ten questions on moving between sources, reading primary authority directly, and building confidence on a sprawling project.

items.q: In multi-source research, what mechanism tells you when to switch sources?
options: The Next Question field of your Research Log: each answer generates a question that may live in a different source
The table of contents of the treatise
items.why: The question in front of you picks the source (Researching Across Sources and the Research Cycle).

options: The statute supplies all the detail
The statute sets the framework, regulations implement it with detail, and case law interprets both
items.why: Missing any one of the three leaves a gap (The Statute-Regulation-Case Law Triangle).

items.q: Why does the chapter insist you open a load-bearing statute in the code rather than rely on a case’s quotation of it?
options: Because cases misquote statutes on purpose
Because the quotation gives you only the language that mattered to that dispute, not the definitions, exceptions, or cross-references
items.why: An excerpt is not the law, and a paraphrase is someone’s interpretation of it (Go to the Source).

items.q: Five consecutive case-law entries in your log on a common-law negligence question is:
options: Quite possibly the research working as designed, since the cases are where the rule lives
A reason to switch to regulations
items.why: The trap is a coverage failure, not a streak of same-type entries (The Single-Source Trap).

items.q: The subtler form of the single-source trap is:
options: An authority type that appears in your log only secondhand, through another source’s characterization, with the primary text never opened
items.why: Every statutory point arriving through a case, every regulatory point through guidance (The Single-Source Trap).

items.q: In the ADA website example, why does the statute alone not settle the question?
options: It was enacted in 1990 and never mentions websites, so the regulation and case law carry the rest
items.why: One question, three source types, each answering what only it can (Answering Questions Across Multiple Sources).

options: Rereading the secondary source that opened the project at the end, with everything you have learned, to catch unpulled threads
Asking a colleague to redo the research
items.why: It turns “nothing new” into documented evidence of coverage (Confidence on a Complex Project).

items.q: When a federal statute and a state common-law rule seem to cover the same conduct, ask first:
options: Whether the federal statute preempts state law expressly or impliedly
Whether the state rule is in a Restatement
items.why: If it does not preempt, both may apply and your analysis addresses each (When Sources Conflict).

items.q: Two habits make the Research Log do coverage work on a multi-source project. One is noting the authority type of each entry. Why?
options: So you can count your entries
So you can audit the log against the map, authority type by authority type, and see what was never reached
So your supervisor can grade it
So the citator can read it
items.why: The research map identifies every authority type in play and becomes the coverage checklist (Managing the Research Log Across Multiple Sources).

items.q: “The law is unsettled” versus “I have not finished looking” is, in the chapter’s words, the difference between:
items.why: Research gap identification is a critical professional skill, and the bar exam tests it too (Chapter Recap).
